articles.title: Fall 2026 Service Change: East King County
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: Starting August 29, King County Metro and Sound Transit will be revising routes on the Eastside. These changes are primarily due to the full 2 Line opening in March 2026. Overall, this restructure is focused on reducing redundant service with the 2 Line while improving frequency and reliability. The Fall 2026 restructure also includes routes in south King County and Pierce County, as well as north King County (will be covered in a future article).
See the full list of changes below or skip to: Central (Bellevue), North (Kirkland/Redmond/Bothell/Woodinville), South (Renton/Mercer Island), East (Issaquah/North Bend), or Night-Owl .

Route 220 is a new route that will travel between Eastgate and downtown Bellevue, via Bellevue College, Lake Hills, and East Main station. During the day, trips will run every 15 minutes on weekdays and every 30 minutes on weekends.

Route 249 will be updated between South Kirkland P&R and downtown Bellevue. Rather than serve Bellevue Way, the route will travel through Medina, Clyde Hill, and Hunts Point. The new Route 270 will provide service on Bellevue Way.

Route 270 is a new route that will travel between downtown Bellevue and the University District, via Bellevue Way and SR-520. The route replaces part of Route 271 and part of Route 249 on north Bellevue Way. During the day, trips will run every 15 minutes on weekdays and every 30 minutes on weekends.
Route 271 will be deleted and replaced by routes 270, 220, and 203.
Route 550 will be deleted and replaced by the 2 Line and Route 556.
Most of the changes for Metro routes in the northeast have already taken effect. The last remaining new route, Route 251, will begin service in Spring 2027 between Redmond and Woodinville.
Route 535 will now run every 30 minutes on Saturday and Sunday. This is a significant improvement from the current 60 minute frequency on Saturday and no Sunday service.

Route 111 will be updated to terminate at South Bellevue and to shorten its loop in East Renton Highlands. Additionally, it will be upgraded from a peak-only route to run all day, everyday at 30 minute frequency (15 minutes during peak).
Route 630 will be slightly revised in First Hill to stop on 9th Ave. Metro is adding one additional inbound trip and two new outbound trips to improve the route’s frequency to 30 minutes.

Route 215 is a new route that will travel between Mercer Island and North Bend, via Eastgate, Issaquah Highlands, and Snoqualmie. Trips will run every 30 minutes between Mercer Island and Issaquah Highlands. Every third trip will continue to North Bend, resulting in a 90 minute frequency between Mercer Island and North Bend. Frequency between Issaquah and North Bend will be improved from 120 minutes to 90 minutes. Additionally, service along this segment will now run on Sunday.

Route 218 will be updated to terminate at Mercer Island. Its frequency will be improved from five peak-direction trips per day to run every 30 minutes in the peak direction between 5:30am to 9:00am and 4:15pm to 7:15pm.

Route 269 will be updated to travel between Marymoor Village and Mercer Island. The route will no longer serve local stops in Issaquah nor the Issaquah Transit Center. Weekday peak frequency will be improved from 30 minutes to 15 minutes. Additionally, this route will now run during the day on weekends.

Route 556 will updated to provide all-day service between Issaquah and Bellevue. The route will provide local service to stops along Front St and Gilman Blvd in Issaquah before running as an express to Eastgate and Bellevue. In Bellevue, Route 556 will serve the stops currently used by Route 550 on Bellevue Way. Trips will run every 15 minutes during the day, everyday.

Route 547 is a new night-owl route between Seattle and Redmond. Running every 30 minutes between midnight and 4:30am, the route will stop near every 2 Line station in this section except for East Main. Passengers traveling to/from Judkins Park, Wilburton, Spring District, Bel-Red, and Overlake Village will need to walk a short distance from the station to bus stop.

articles.title: Wilson Launches Housing Task Force, Pledging to Streamline Permitting
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: Mayor Katie Wilson rolled out an executive order pledging to streamline Seattle's building permitting process on Wednesday. In addition to two immediate actions aimed at reducing permit times, the order launched a Housing Production Task Force to advise the city's future housing agenda.

"We're taking two immediate actions," Wilson said. "One of those is the interdepartmental team on permitting, which is going to better coordinate our City departments to shorten permit timelines, and then proposing funding in the budget for next year for the affordable housing ombuds that can help our developers navigate those processes."

The mayor's housing task force "will bring together communities most impacted by City policy to craft recommendations to build needed housing, support affordable and community‑based developers, prevent displacement, and attract development to Seattle," according to a press release timed with the roll out.

Housing starts have been in a nosedive in Seattle after a boom period that lasted more than a decade, allowing Seattle's population to grow beyond 820,000 residents . The Emerald City's housing starts collapsed to a decade-long low of fewer than 2,000 units permitted in 2025 – down 88% from the 2020 peak of 17,400 units permitted.

Builders have pointed to a number of factors that create a drag on homebuilding, including high interest rates, high construction costs, and waning interest from financers – some of which are beyond the City's control. Permitting delays and fees are something the City does control, however, leading to calls for streamlining.

“Housing that people can afford is critical to a city that works for everyone," Wilson said. "We can't control every force that drives up the cost of building homes, but we can act where it counts. This Executive Order is about clearing the path, cutting the delays, and building the housing Seattle needs — now.”
The task force is expected to be a large one and cut across sectors, likely encompassing more than 60 members. Three of the four co-chairs appeared at the press conference alongside the mayor.

The four co-chairs are Carter Nelson, Director of Government Affairs with the Commercial Real Estate Development Association, Joel Ing, principle of Edge Developers, and Tiffany Kelly-Gray, Director of Strategic Initiatives at Byrd Barr Place, and Seattle Councilmember Eddie Lin, who chairs Council's Land Use Committee.

"This task force is going to be providing rolling recommendations," Wilson said. "There will be initial recommendations provided in February of 2027 that we will be able to act on next year. I also want to emphasize: This is not 'instead of.' This is in addition to the many other housing-related processes and activities that our departments are already doing."

The first question during the press scrum pressed the mayor on what announcing a task force not set to deliver recommendations until next year does to build more housing immediately. The mayor responded by pointing to the housing actions she has already taken, including her recent ordinance banning rental junk fees and her "Taller Faster Denser" housing plan , which aims to expand the city's housing capacity well beyond the growth plan her predecessor, Bruce Harrell, laid out.

"I just want to emphasize that we have not waited until this point to take action on housing affordability," Wilson said. "The city council just unanimously passed our ordinance banning rental junk fees, which will improve stability and affordability for renters, and we're also working on a larger scoping for the next phase of the Comprehensive Plan, so that we have more options for increasing housing production across the city. So this is additive, and we are not waiting for September 2027 to take action."

One Wilson initiative that did not make it out of the gates in her first eight months in office is the "Housing Accelerator" pilot program , which had similarly been touted as a measure to spur housing production. The idea was that a temporary two-year break in Mandatory Housing Affordability (MHA) fees, floated as an 80% reduction, would convince builders sitting on permits to break ground, encompassing several thousand homes.

However, the deal fell apart after the Housing Development Consortium, which represents a wide range of nonprofit builders and their partners, pulled their support and backing from key city councilmembers also appeared in jeopardy. This led Wilson to pull the legislation, pledging to bring it back next year. That MHA break proposal now appears to ride on making it into the consensus recommendations of the Housing Production Task Force.

At the task force roll out, The Urbanist asked if reducing MHA fees and curbing rising utility fees that the City is heaping on builders would be on the agenda. Wilson seemed to suggest it would be a discussion point, but stopped short of promising any particular outcome or making it a focal point.
"I think that's something that the task force will be able to discuss," Wilson said.

The mayor's executive order seeks to reduce delays stemming from City departments, but it's unclear if the effort will tackle utility infrastructure costs, which industry professionals have flagged as a growing issue stunting building.

As it stands, the Mayor’s Office says it is launching a "Residential Permitting Interdepartmental Team to make permit timelines shorter and more predictable across all regulatory departments involved in most housing construction projects." Additionally, the mayor has directed Seattle City Light, the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT), the Seattle Fire Department, and Seattle Public Utilities to each designate a primary point of contact for interdepartmental coordination to quickly resolve permitting issues for applicants.
Patience Malaba, the Housing Development Consortium's Executive Director, also spoke at the event, and noted the boost the effort could provide for nonprofit builders.

“For affordable housing, delays have real consequences," Malaba said. "When permits stall, costs rise. The Affordable Housing Ombudsperson and Interdepartmental Team can help create the coordination and accountability needed to keep projects moving. Clear points of contact across SDCI, Seattle City Light, SDOT, Seattle Fire, and Seattle Public Utilities can help resolve problems earlier and give housing providers greater certainty.”

The press conference was well attended, but the TV newscasters who dominated the Q&A session quickly pivoted to their preferred topic of pressing the mayor about the pushback and fledgling recall effort she is facing following the Bite of Seattle shooting . In contrast, their interest in diving into housing issues appeared pretty thin.
Builders from both the private and nonprofit sectors invited to take part in Wednesday's event were bullish that the task force could achieve the mayor's lofty aims.

"We appreciate Mayor Wilson and her team's leadership in convening this group," Nelson said. "Bringing together community leaders, nonprofits, housing advocates, and industry professionals is exactly the kind of collaboration we need to approach a challenge as complex as housing affordability. We're grateful to have a seat at the table and look forward to working with this group to identify the key barriers that make housing more difficult. We're excited to help advance practical solutions that make it easier to deliver housing for current and future Seattleites."
Ing noted the new task force will be building on the work of a previous task force former Mayor Ed Murray set to work in 2014.

"Following upon the efforts 10 years ago of the Housing Affordability and Livability Agenda task force to increase housing production, also known as HALA," Ing said. "Now is the time to refine many of those strategies while developing new initiatives. The housing shortage continues to worsen in our city, as we all know, and the region. So, the opportunity to improve many development requirements that prevent and challenge this housing production is both welcome and needed."

The HALA committee helped engineer the MHA inclusionary zoning program, which traded upzones for requirements for affordable housing contributions from builders. That cleared the way for the associated upzones in urban centers across Seattle, which started in 2017 and were completed in 2019 . However, the HALA committee and Mayor Murray abandoned a plan to phase out single family zoning citywide after the draft proposal was leaked to the Seattle Times , whose columnists savaged the idea , kicking up a homeowner backlash.

As a result, it took a state mandate contained within Rep. Jess Bateman's Middle Housing Law to bring about an end to single family zoning – in Seattle's case, right before the state deadline in June 2025.

Whether Wilson's new task force, more than a decade later, can operate with fewer untimely leaks and policy setbacks remains to be seen. Whether market-rate builders, nonprofit leaders, and tenant advocates will see eye to eye on housing policy is a dicey proposition as well.

Regardless of the outcome, a task force has been birthed into existence, summoning the powers of the Seattle Process, whether creative or dilatory, and bringing them to bear on a problem widely agreed to be pressing and crucial to Seattle's ability to thrive over coming decades.

articles.title: First Hill apartment homicide victim identified as 28-year-old
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: The King County Medical Examiner’s Office has identified the 28-year-old shot and killed inside a First Hill apartment building Tuesday night as Gador Peter Wal .
Wal died from multiple gunshot wounds, and the Medical Examiner officially ruled the death of the Seattle man a homicide.

CHS reported here as Seattle Police and Seattle Fire medics responded just after 8:00 PM Tuesday to 911 reports of a shooting victim found inside the address of the M Street Apartments in the 900 block of 8th Ave.

According to East Precinct radio updates, Wal was found unresponsive and badly injured in a unit of the building. Arriving officers began CPR until Seattle Fire arrived but the victim was declared dead at the scene.
Officers cordoned off the area around 8th Ave and Madison, canvassing the building and surrounding blocks for witnesses and surveillance footage.

No arrests have been announced and the Seattle Police Department Homicide Unit continues to investigate the shooting. Anyone with information is asked to contact the SPD Violent Crimes Tip Line at (206) 233-5000.
Seattle has recorded 22 homicides so far in 2026.

articles.title: Suspect charged as prosecutors say Cal Anderson shooting that sent man to hospital was accident
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: A 29-year-old man faces felony charges after an accidental shooting at Cal Anderson Park left his friend “bleeding profusely” from the leg earlier this month, according to King County Superior Court charging documents.
Prosecutors charged Mark Paul with third-degree assault with a firearm enhancement and first-degree unlawful possession of a firearm.
CHS reported here on the Monday night, August 10th shooting along Nagle Place next to the park’s basketball courts.

While standing beside a parked SUV containing an adult and two children, Paul allegedly attempted to clear a handgun by racking the slide, according to the charges. The weapon reportedly discharged into the ground, sending a bullet fragment into the leg of a man he was talking with. The victim suffered heavy bleeding and was transported to Harborview Medical Center .

Paul fled the scene on foot and was arrested a few hours later after a witness spotted him outside an E Pike Street smoke shop. Authorities noted Paul was legally prohibited from possessing firearms due to multiple past felony convictions, including first-degree robbery, and had more than 20 prior warrants.
Police say the handgun from the shooting was not recovered.

The charging documents reveal other details of the case including how a woman driving a white SUV was detained downtown after police followed her vehicle leaving the scene with an adult and two children inside. Officers found an unfired bullet in her vehicle and determined probable cause to arrest her for reckless endangerment and third-degree driving with a suspended license. The woman said she was the suspect’s girlfriend but claimed he had not been the vehicle the night of the shooting.

It is still unclear if there was a second shooting victim at Harborview on the night from a separate incident or if there was confusion about the man accidentally shot by Paul. CHS has been unable to learn more from the authorities about the second report at the emergency room.
Paul pleaded not guilty at his August 18 arraignment, where a judge denied a motion to reduce his $25,000 bail. He remains jailed with a trial scheduled for October.

articles.title: The Stranger’s Exhaustively Comprehensive Bursting-at-the Seams Guide to Bumbershoot 2026!
articles.author: Megan Seling
paras: Phew! Another music festival? But it’s almost September! Isn’t it time to go back to school and drink hot cocoa under a cozy blanket and pretend to care about football?

No! There is still summer fun to be had, as exhausted as you may be, because Bumbershoot is taking over the Seattle Center September 5 and 6 with two days of music, comedy, art, wrestling, fashion, and so much more. (Like, literally there is a mermaid???)

We know how overwhelming festivals can be, and this year’s Bumbershoot line-up, while smaller than previous iterations, is still loaded with so much good shit. Bikini Kill! De La Soul! Noname! Peaches! So we did your homework for you and wrote up every! single! band! playing over the weekend, as well as all the fun arts and culture and cat stuff. We even put big fat stars next to stuff you definitely can’t miss.

Have some downtime before your favorites hit the stage? Flip through these pages to find fun games like Mad Libs, a musical word search, and a thrilling round of Who Said It?, in which you can test your knowledge of gothic prose and ask yourself: Is this an Edgar Allan Poe poem or a Death Cab for Cutie song?
Who Said It: Edgar Allan Poe or Ben Gibbard?
Creative Direction & Design Corianton Hale
The post The Stranger’s Exhaustively Comprehensive Bursting-at-the Seams Guide to Bumbershoot 2026! appeared first on The Stranger .

articles.title: Every Band Playing Bumbershoot: Saturday
articles.author: Megan Seling, Rob Moura, Sam Machkovech, Audrey Vann, Julianne Bell, Rachel Stevens, and Charles Mudede
paras: ⭐ 📍 ANTHERS This comparison will only resonate with maybe six people, but I’m gonna say it anyway: If you loved long-defunct Seattle punk rock noise makers pleasureboaters, go see ANTHERS and party like you’re at Healthy Times Fun Club circa 2008. Not a 40-something who lived in Seattle nearly two decades ago? Fine. Here are some more rock bona fides—ANTHERS’ latest singles, “Soup” and “Collector,” were recorded by Ben Verellen of Helms Alee and Joel Cuplin of Constant Lovers. And in 2024, The Stranger ’s contributing concert photographer Brittne Lunniss—who attends hundreds of shows a year—said the band delivered one of her favorite performances, writing, “ANTHERS was the best car crash I’ve ever been in.” Hell yes. ( Upper Courtyard Stage ) MEGAN SELING

📍 Aryana León In a 2024 interview, Aryana León recalls standing in front of the mirror as a young teen, practicing her “lightsaber introduction” as if she were a star on the Disney Channel. Today, she’s flourishing as a pop/R&B artist on the rise, having played her first Capitol Hill Block Party in 2024 and releasing her first EP, PLEASURE , in 2025. Her voice is incredible, warm currents over songs that play like smooth passenger-side car rides by the bay—perfect for a late August day under the shade of the Needle. ( Upper Courtyard Stage ) ROB MOURA

📍 Bexley Lead singer Amanda Hardy is the dark-hair-in-her-eyes girl at your high school who exclusively wore baggy Alice in Chains and Soundgarden T-shirts. Her band Bexley keeps that spirit alive by fusing overdriven, heavy riffs, soulful wails over guitar solos, and a Zeppelin/Sabbath foundation of ’70s rock. Your dad will tap his toes, and you might bang your head. We hope to hear “Female Hysteria” in Bexley’s Bumbershoot set, as its core, Nirvana-like riff evolves into a Kim Thayil–worthy guitar upswell. ( Upper Courtyard Stage ) SAM MACHKOVECH

⭐ 📍 Bikini Kill When Bikini Kill embarked on their first reunion tour in 2019, I traveled to Los Angeles to see it, fearing it’d be a one-time thing. (They’ve since performed approximately 10 million times in cities way closer to me, but I’m not bitter about it, I swear.) See, the Olympia feminist punk band is the reason I went to Evergreen State College; the reason I wasn’t afraid to stand up to know-it-all dudes at said college; the reason I ironed the words “kill me” on a Forever 21 dress in high school. Despite my riot grrl phase blossoming in the 2010s, lyrics to their early ’90s songs like “There are no boundaries on what I can feel” (“Feels Blind”) and “Don’t need you to tell us we’re good / Don’t need you to say we suck / Don’t need your protection / Don’t need your dick to fuck” (“Don’t Need You”) were still just as fresh, jolting, and resonant as they were two (and now three) decades before. ( Mural Stage ) AUDREY VANN

⭐ Blood Orange It’s been 10 years since Dev Hynes, aka Blood Orange, dropped his iconic album Freetown Sound , and I, for one, have never been the same. The lush, dreamy ’80s R&B- and funk-influenced songs soundtracked a sun-soaked summer in my 20s and seeped into my memories. Hynes has collaborated with artists as diverse as Britney Spears, Solange Knowles, Tinashe, Carly Rae Jepsen, Debbie Harry, Sky Ferreira, and Mariah Carey. His last album, Essex Honey , is a meditation on grief and his upbringing in Essex, as well as how music has bolstered him throughout his life. I just know that his Bumbershoot set is going to heal me. ( Fisher Stage ) JULIANNE BELL

⭐ Cain Culto Are you ready to party your ass off? Because no one can do it like a gay icon who used to be an evangelical worship pastor. Born Andrew Padilla, this alt-artist started going by “Cain” as a reference to two things: (1) Cain in the Bible, the scripture’s first recorded bad boy; and (2) the Spanish word for “worship” is “cain,” which hearkens to his Colombian and Nicaraguan heritage. Cain Culto raps, sings, and plays electric violin while dancing like you’re on the floor at your favorite gay bar. While it’s pop music meets Latin rap, there is still an element of worship in Cain Culto’s music. Except now, he’s not asking you to follow Jesus, he’s singing of queer joy and “Uh, fuck Trump, fuck ICE, free Palestine. I’ma say that shit again: free Palestine.” Hallelujah! ( Mural Stage ) RACHEL STEVENS

Chase & Status If Turnstile’s hardcore isn’t your thing, head over to the Mural Stage where London-based DJs Chase & Status (aka Saul Milton and Will Kennard) will close out Saturday night with what’s sure to devolve into a dizzying drum ‘n’ bass dance party. No, they haven’t won a Grammy like Turnstile, but they have won a Brit Award, which is the UK equivalent. Pick your poison. ( Mural Stage ) MEGAN SELING

Die Spitz Die Spitz popped off—first in their home city of Austin, then nationwide—based on their live performances wherein the band’s all-femme roster would trade vocal leads and put out punk so incendiary it would damn near burn the venue down. After winning their local Album of the Year award (someone should start that here!) for their ferocious 2023 EP Teeth , they secured opening slots for bands like Sleater-Kinney and Amyl and the Sniffers. For better and worse, the group has hype coming out of their pores; fans of loud music should strongly consider catching their set. ( Fisher Stage ) ROB MOURA

Joey Valence & Brae Joey Valence & Brae have been collecting Beastie Boys comparisons for years, at least since releasing their 2023 full-length Punk Tactics , and I wanted to hate it, tbh. But their chaotic punk-laced hip-hop tracks that, yes, sound very much like the Beastie Boys and the days when rockstars and rappers collaborated are bursting with sincerity. They sound less like a rip-off and more like a whole-hearted celebration of all the musicians who inspired them to pick up a mic. Hard to be mad at that. ( Fisher Stage ) MEGAN SELING

📍 Juliet Daniel Ever wonder what quitting your tech job at Microsoft to make bedroom pop would sound like? It sounds like Juliet Daniel, because that’s what this hero did. Daniel’s boppable music was born and bred in Seattle, and it sounds like taking the leaps we all want to make but probably aren’t confident enough to take. This sentiment shines brightest while flooded with 2000s nostalgia in the singer-songwriter’s song “Stare You Down.” The parting lyrics would be everywhere on AIM away messages, if only we were all still doing that: If you don’t {want me} ~*~*~I think you’re crazy~*~*~ ( Upper Courtyard Stage ) RACHEL STEVENS

⭐ Lucy Dacus Out of the three boygeniuses, I’ve always had an affinity for Lucy Dacus. With her introspective, storytelling lyrics and her impressive Goodreads profile, she’s truly a writer’s musician. I love the depictions of nascent queerness in songs like “Kissing Lessons” and “Christine,” the crackling slow burn of “Night Shift,” and the righteous fury of “Thumbs.” Her 2025 album, Forever Is a Feeling , finds the singer-songwriter in her hopeless romantic era, with swoony, intimate ballads like “Best Guess” and “Ankles.” I attended her Remlinger Farms performance last summer and watched her officiate a wedding ceremony for seven couples during the show, which will be a difficult feat to top—nevertheless, I’m eager to see what she has in store for Bumbershoot. ( Fisher Stage ) JULIANNE BELL

📍 Meat Hair If you love local Sub Pop darlings Deep Sea Diver (and who doesn’t?), then definitely don’t miss Meat Hair, an experimental jam band in which members of DSD get real weird. ( Upper Courtyard Stage ) MEGAN SELING

Molchat Doma Minsk, the capital of Belarus, is a weird city of contrasts: gold-lined facades on its main streets, and gothic counterculture seeping in its Eastern European shadows. Dark-wave trio Molchat Doma thus sound appropriately Belarusian. Bearded men hunch over synthesizers and guitars—and occasionally a standing, dance-friendly electric drum kit—to bang out shimmering-yet-devilish techno that sprinkles Gregorian chant into New Order’s formula. Don a trench coat and dance darkly, fellow mavens of the night. ( Mural Stage ) SAM MACHKOVECH

⭐ 📍 Oblé Reed Oblé Reed made the most of Seattle’s post-pandemic plate shift, rushing into the city’s devastated hip-hop scene via a tsunami of well-produced, well-written hip-hop titled LINDENAVE! He followed that up with an equally compelling visual EP ( Retrovision ) and a second album on which he broke local containment and brought even more underrated national talent into the fold ( LINE LEADERS ). Today, it’s safe to say that the 24-year-old artist is near the top of the most notable rappers to spawn from our waterlogged loam this decade. Considering he’s one of the few rappers at this year’s Bumbershoot (besides fellow local hero Travis Thompson), you owe it to yourself to see the man work a crowd. ( Upper Courtyard Stage ) ROB MOURA

⭐ Peaches It’s 2026, and we need Peaches’ sexually transgressive electroclash hip-hop more than ever. Luckily, the feminist musician, director, and performance artist returned this year with her first album in over ten years, No Lube So Rude . “When the world is friction, lube isn’t a luxury. It’s a necessity,” Peaches writes. “It’s how you turn that friction into pleasure, into power, into pride.” The icon’s seventh album does just as advertised by acting as a relieving salve for these dry times, slickening the constant thrust of dystopian news with empowering, funny, and celebratory tracks for the dance floor like “Fuck How You Wanna Fuck” and “Not in Your Mouth None of Your Business.” I haven’t seen her on this tour yet, so just take it from Reddit user Senhoegahara, who wrote, “This girl has CRAZY energy. She put on a helluva show. Couldn’t believe she’s almost 60. She was topless the entire show and crowdsurfed for a good 10 whole minutes. Lmfao.” ( Mural Stage ) AUDREY VANN

Pixel Grip If you’ve been looking for a tighter, gayer, and synthier version of Yeah Yeah Yeahs, Chicago trio Pixel Grip would like to slowly sidle up to you at a very sweaty nightclub. Their drums-and-Moog brand of fist-pumping dance-pop might not befit a sunny Seattle Center stage, but their chunky, brzzt-brzzt Moog-synth jams may be worth slapping on your favorite sunglasses and black leather before stomping along to bangers like “Dancing on Your Grave.” ( Fisher Stage ) SAM MACHKOVECH

⭐ 📍 Sera Cahoone *Picture the old lady from Titanic here* It’s been 14 years… since Sera Cahoone has played Bumbershoot! She’s basically writing directly to us with her brand-new album (out August 28, 2026), titled I’ve Missed You All These Years . Girl, we’ve missed you, too! Cahoone’s new music feels like it’s infused with a newfound joy that only comes from the other side of really going through it. Of the new album, Cahoone says, “I want people to feel what I felt and put themselves in the way I felt back then. I want them to think, ‘If she made it through, I can too.’” If you don’t yet know the magic of Sera Cahoone’s blues meets folk meets country, it’s never too late to pull up a chair. If you’ve been a fan for decades, welcome home. ( Upper Courtyard Stage ) RACHEL STEVENS

Silvana Estrada Mexican singer-songwriter Silvana Estrada combines the sparse acoustic guitars and romantic poetry of South American folk revivalist artists Violeta Parra and Mercedes Sosa with the vocal chops of American jazz icons Billie Holiday and Sarah Vaughn. (For fans of Joan Baez, Angel Olsen, and crying at concerts.) ( Mural Stage ) AUDREY VANN

⭐ 📍 Travis Thompson In 2022, the gifted Burien rapper Travis Thompson made a little history by appearing, alongside Marc Maron, on what was then the coolest TV show, Reservation Dogs. Soon after this exposure, Thompson, who is part Navajo, released a music video for his slamming track “Corner Store.” It featured Macklemore, the last superstar rapper to come straight out of this city. Thompson also dropped the NW hip-hop classic “Need You.” Whatever you do, do not sleep on this cat. ( Fisher Stage ) CHARLES MUDEDE

⭐ Turnstile Since their formation in 2010, the Baltimore-based hardcore punk band Turnstile have grown from hometown darling to mainstream breakout success, taking home two Grammys in February and drawing praise from the likes of Hayley Williams and fellow Saturday headliner Dev Hynes of Blood Orange. The group counts Bad Brains and Sade among their influences and mixes hardcore with melodic pop structures to irresistible effect. They’re especially known for their high-octane, mosh-heavy performances, which many fans describe as life-changing. I saw them at WAMU Theater last October, and the sense of joy and community in the room was palpable—I can’t wait to experience it again. ( Fisher Stage ) JULIANNE BELL

XCOMM Teenagers? Playing music!? And it’s good ???? It will never not be hilarious when grown-ass music critics realize that teens can play guitars. XCOMM from Los Angeles are the music industry’s current “omg they’re so young!” obsession. Their blistering skate punk is thrashy, fast, and injected with some nu-metal guitar wailing, and it doesn’t hurt that their debut full-length, Time to Burn , was recorded by Ross Robinson, who’s worked with bands like the Blood Brothers, Korn, and Slipknot. And yes, the drummer is like 14. Get over it. ( Mural Stage ) MEGAN SELING

articles.title: Sammamish Poised to Pivot Away from Town Center Growth This Fall
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Councilmembers in the sleepy Eastside bedroom city that is Sammamish face a crucial decision later this fall, in the wake of council elections that tilted the balance of power away from its previous pro-density direction. The impact of the decision will likely be felt for years to come, as city leaders decide whether to step away from a plan that was intended to finally foster the beleaguered Town Center area into something closer to a real downtown for a city of nearly 70,000.

Incorporated in 1999, Sammamish has been trying to foster some type of center city for its entire (albeit brief) existence. In 2008, after years of debate, the council approved a Town Center plan that capped development at 2,000 housing units, despite capacity for many more across 240 acres.

Very little of that plan, which envisioned separate mixed-use "nodes" far away from the main thoroughfare of 228th Avenue SE, came to fruition. One reason was very meager density limits, with developers like the builders of the Village at Sammamish Town Center (home to Metropolitan Market) consolidating their projects on a portion of a lot in order to be able to build up.

"When the Town Center was originally adopted, it was envisioned in part as a place to put the growth. However, the opposite, you could argue, actually happened, and instead of growth happening in the town center, the growth continued to happen as infill in the neighborhoods in the form of single-family residential subdivisions," Sammamish Community Development Director David Pyle said last month.

A few months before the November election, the Sammamish Council voted 6 to 1 to advance study of a growth alternative for Town Center that would have increased the upper limit on the number of units that could be built from 2,000 – where it has stood for nearly two decades – to 4,000. The move was intended to be a step toward creating development standards that allow a mixed-use neighborhood to take shape, rather than Sammamish's current glide path toward more townhouse development in the so-called city center.

Then the voters weighed in, sweeping two pro-density councilmembers out of office and tilting the balance of power away from the bloc that had voted yes last year. In a campaign season that had focused heavily on the Town Center issue, all three councilmembers who took office in January had opposed the idea of studying 4,000 units in explicit terms, citing issues like traffic, infrastructure costs, and "unchecked development."

Josh Amato, who was selected by the new growth-skeptical majority to be mayor in January, had included a banner at the top of his campaign website that read "Josh is opposed to the 4,000 unit upzone in the Town Center."

Now the city has to decide how to move forward, but doing nothing and fully abandoning the Town Center plan isn't an option. Without some density increases within the city, Sammamish doesn't have enough capacity for households across lower income bands, a directive spelled out in House Bill 1220 , which the state legislature passed in 2021.

Moreover, City leaders are eyeing the new Housing Accountability Act , in which the state's Commerce Department reviews the growth plans in select cities to make sure that they're in compliance, and they don't want to end up on the watch list alongside places like Carnation and Bainbridge Island . Before moving to pass an emergency ordinance to get into compliance, Bainbridge had been flirting with triggering the Builder's Remedy, which would have superseded local zoning to allow much greater height and density when builders include a set amount of affordable housing.

In July, city staff sought direction from the Sammamish Planning Commission, with commissioners expressing a clear interest in an "option 4" that would take planned capacity increases in Town Center and distribute that to the city's other commercial centers, like Klahanie, Pine Lake, and Inglewood.

"The biggest advantage of option four, is if you spread it over six or seven [...] different neighborhood centers or subareas, you distribute the traffic, which has been the major, major opposition of the community, going from 2,000 to 4,000, because the town center basically infrastructure is not there to support even the 2,000," commission vice chair Seyed Safavian said.
Safavian noted that Klahanie, currently home to a QFC grocery store, is well-positioned when it comes to a Sound Transit light rail station in Central Issaquah.

"Klahanie has perfect access, and within 5, 10 minutes... access to the freeway, access to the future transit, and Klahanie has really very good roads, road capacity, intersections, roadway improvement infrastructure, and all that that really helps us a lot as far as accepting more housing units, particularly for affordable housing," Safavian said.

Ultimately, it will be up to the Sammamish Council to decide how to proceed, with some moves this year signaling the new majority's potential direction. A unanimous vote last month removes a policy from the city's Comprehensive Plan that would have pushed the city to pursue a designation as a regional growth center, a move that could have unlocked more infrastructure funding for the city – and likely come with requirements for more density.

Just this week, the council voted 5-2 to overhaul its affordability requirements in low-density residential areas, essentially gutting a fee in-lieu program that was intended to act as something of a check on the city's continued proliferation of large single-family homes. Previously, all new homes over 1,500 square feet were required to pay a fee that would be used to fund affordable housing, but that threshold was raised to 1,750 square feet – with the fee only applying to square footage exceeding that threshold.
But the looming Town Center vote will likely be the most pivotal of the year, determining how Sammamish grows for at least a decade.

"Trying what we tried from before, we will end up with the same opposition that we faced from before. It's the same community, it's the same people. Let's try something different," planning commissioner Hisham Elkhawad said. "You said it needs more work. I would rather do the more work and succeed at the end of it instead of trying what we tried, and we failed."
Correction: an earlier version of this article incorrectly stated that three councilmembers lost their reelection bid last year, but the number is two: one seat was an open race.

articles.title: Op-Ed: How Pike Place Market Can Thrive in the Winter Without Car Traffic
articles.author: Gordon Padelford
paras: Seattleites love Pike Place Market, but hate random vehicle traffic pushing through the heart of it. That has been clear over and over again in surveys and polls, so it has come as a shock that the City is proposing to allow all car traffic Monday to Thursday from October through March .

The latest survey from the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT), conducted this past June, heard from 5,403 people and found “98% Support: Near-universal community backing for vehicle barriers.” Importantly, the survey also heard “96% Business Agreement: High alignment among local merchants and staff” among 224 respondents.

Limiting general car traffic in the Market is as close to complete political consensus as Seattle is going to get on anything. Support spans the spectrum of Seattle politics from The Stranger and Mayor Wilson, to the Seattle Times and former Mayor Bruce Harrell.
And let’s be clear about what we’re talking about when we say “limiting general-purpose car traffic” or “pedestrianization.”

No one is seriously proposing preventing businesses from loading and unloading (regardless of whether businesses are using personal or commercial vehicles to do so), deliveries from reaching the Market, or emergency vehicles from responding when needed.

We’re talking about restricting unnecessary vehicle trips: tour buses, Ubers, lost tourists rubbernecking in rentals, and visitors who want to drive and park on the street for their personal convenience.
Limiting this unnecessary traffic makes Pike Place more functional, and makes room for what makes Pike Place special.

During the pilot, the Market has continued to function as both a loading dock and a front porch — a place where farmers can vend in the street, musicians can busk, visitors can sit and gather, and businesses can receive the deliveries they need to operate.
The good news is that, overall, the pilot has been successful :

But unfortunately there were never any agreed on success metrics for the pilot, so the debate about it seems to be endless and anecdotal. The latest news is a proposal to scale back the pilot to allow more vehicles on the street Monday through Thursday starting this fall through the early spring — why?

The issue seems to be that a subset of businesses say some of their driving customers are buying less because they find it inconvenient or expensive to park in the attached 800-stall public car parking garage ( Urban Freight Lab memo ). Exactly how many discouraged driving customers we are talking about is not clear. The Urban Freight Lab study found in a survey of 2,546 visitors to the Market that only 14.5% of customers drive (85.5% walk, bike, or take transit), but how many of those feel discouraged by having to park in the garage seems to be unknown — so we’re stuck with anecdotal concerns that seems to be driving this decision (pun intended).
The good news is that there are alternative solutions to retain these picky driving customers instead of opening Pike Place back up to general purpose traffic !

Taking this approach would make for a better shopping experience for the 85.5% of customers who don’t drive, and open up possibilities to grow the customer base even more. Last fall, we interviewed five pedestrianized markets in Cincinnati , Burlington , Boulder , Charlottesville , and London to learn how they stay active and vibrant all winter long. Here are a few possibilities inspired by those conversations:
Pedestrianization would also mean more space for vendors to safely load and unload on the street.
It would mean parents can shop with their children without worrying about random car traffic.
It would mean people with disabilities can walk or roll in the street without worrying about whether they will be seen by a backing-up tourist in a rental SUV.

It would mean that Pike Place is more than a parking lot — it’s both the loading dock and the front porch of the heart of Seattle. It’s a destination for the public to visit, shop, gather, and build community. It’s no wonder 98% of Seattleites want to keep it prioritized for people — the real question is why can’t our governance structures deliver a better Pike Place for everyone?

You can ask them by emailing your thoughts to: Pike Place Market Historical Commission MinhChau.Le@seattle.gov >, Pike Place Market Preservation and Development Authority (PDA) info@pikeplacemarket.org >, SDOT Director angela.brady@seattle.gov >, and Mayor of Seattle mayor.wilson@seattle.gov >.

articles.title: All aboard Amtrak’s sleeker, cleaner new trains
articles.author: Benton Graham
paras: On Charlie Hamilton’s regular Amtrak rides from Seattle to Portland, Oregon, and Vancouver, British Columbia, he passes some of the country’s most spectacular vistas: the Puget Sound coast and the Skagit Valley. On clear days, he can even see Mount Rainier. But perhaps the most beautiful sight is not the natural wonders of the Pacific Northwest. It’s the cars and trucks inching along the highway.

“It’s nice to be able to be going along there and going faster than what people on Interstate 5 are doing. We kind of like that bit,” said Hamilton, who leads the train advocacy organization All Aboard Washington.

Indeed, riding the train in the Pacific Northwest can take about as long as driving. The trip between Seattle and Portland takes about 3 hours and 30 minutes by either mode, even though the train makes six stops along the way.

Amtrak plans to begin rolling out 83 new trainsets, dubbed Airo , this fall, starting with eight on the Pacific Northwest’s Cascades route. The trains will eventually serve more than a dozen routes in places like New England, Pennsylvania, and much of the mid-Atlantic region. The $8-billion investment is expected to reduce trip times on multiple routes, though Amtrak did not say by how much, and the trains can reach speeds of up to 125 mph. The Cascades trains will also carry 317 passengers — significantly more than the current Cascades rolling stock — and will boost reliability and comfort, according to an Amtrak spokesperson.

Improved hardware could also help advance All Aboard Washington’s vision of more frequent rail service in the region. “Having trains once an hour would be very helpful, and the Airo trainsets would make it possible to do that,” Hamilton said.

The Airo trains also represent a significant and long overdue refresh for Amtrak, which still has trains that date to the 1970s. The carrier has said the new hardware will provide “significant environmental benefits” while making the rider experience more pleasant. The rollout follows the introduction of new NextGen Acela trains on the Northeast Corridor last summer.

Amtrak’s refresh comes after the Biden administration made a historic $66 billion investment in passenger and freight rail through the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act. But it arrives at a tumultuous moment. Despite Amtrak setting ridership records for two consecutive years, the Trump administration has proposed severe cuts to passenger rail funding. Still, the federal government did announce $3 billion in funding, including $2 billion to purchase trains, for Amtrak in August.

Rail carries 8 percent of the world’s passengers, yet accounts for just 2 percent of global transportation energy demand. In that sense, the Airo trains will help make a clean form of transport even cleaner.

Alex Scott, a professor of supply chain management at the University of Tennessee-Knoxville, said rail’s efficiency comes in part from carrying many people at once. “If you can get a fully well-utilized rail car, be it humans or products, those are still more efficient than everybody going in different cars, even if they’re electric cars,” he said.

The trains, built in the U.S. by Siemens , feature electric and diesel propulsion, allowing them to operate on both conventional and electrified routes. While much of the U.S. passenger rail network remains unelectrified, employing new diesel-powered trains can still reduce emissions. “The locomotives they make now, even if they’re not electric, are a heck of a lot cleaner than the old ones, and so upgrading equipment, be it electric or not, is a good answer,” Scott said.

Airo locomotives meet the Environmental Protection Agency’s Tier 4 emissions standards — the agency’s strictest rules for locomotive engines — significantly reducing particulate matter and nitrogen oxide emissions.

Riders on the Northeast Regional route will climb aboard Airo trains in 2027. The new rolling stock will especially benefit riders traveling between Virginia and the Northeast who can wait as long as an hour at Union Station in Washington, D.C. while Amtrak swaps the diesel engine it uses south of the capital to the electric one it uses northbound to Boston. The new trains can quickly transition from diesel to electric power without changing locomotives.

“It’s a win for the environment, it’s a win for the people that are sitting in traffic,” Virginia Passenger Rail Authority spokesperson Karina Romero said. “We definitely want more trains in Virginia.”

Virginia has invested $6 billion in its Transforming Rail in Virginia program. According to Romero, the combination of new trains and improved infrastructure will give riders a more reliable experience.
“You can put down fabulous infrastructure and great tracks,” she said, “but you’ve definitely got to have the equipment to roll on.”
This story was originally published by Grist with the headline All aboard Amtrak’s sleeker, cleaner new trains on Aug 19, 2026.

articles.title: Fall 2026 Service Change: Pierce County and South King County
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: Starting August 29, King County Metro, Sound Transit, and Pierce Transit will be making changes to bus routes in south King County and Pierce County. Most of these changes are in response to the Federal Link Link Extension that opened in December 2025. Service changes in east and north King County will be discussed in future articles.

Across this sub-region, the biggest change is Sound Transit’s Route 574. Route 574 will be truncated at Federal Way Downtown station (instead of SeaTac) and will now run every 15 minutes. At the southern end of the route, the stop at Lakewood Transit Center will be replaced by a stop at Lakewood station.

Routes throughout south King and Pierce Counties will be adjusted in a few weeks. See full list of changes below, or skip to Burien and SeaTac , Kent and Des Moines , Auburn and Federal Way , Pierce County , or Night-Owl changes.

Route 121 will be partially restored to provide eight peak hour trips (four AM and four PM) between Burien Transit Center and downtown Seattle. This route will take just 37 minutes compared to 53 minutes on the H Line.

Route 156 will have a slightly revised routing on its trips between Southcenter and Kent Des Moines station. The route will no longer serve the McMicken Heights loop (dashed blue line on the map). The route will also have expanded service, running from 4am to 11pm on weekdays and 4:30am to 11pm on weekends.
DART Route 631 will now have weekend service. The route will operate the same schedule on Saturday and Sunday as it does during the week.

Route 164 is a new route that will replace the southern half of the current Route 165. Route 164 will run every 15 minutes during the day, every day. Some of the route’s northbound trips will continue to Route 166. Route 166 replaces the northern segment of Route 165. Buses will run every 15 minutes during peak hours and every 30 minutes during the rest of the day. Every southbound trip will continue to Route 164.
Route 168 will have a few additional trips added to provide 15 minute frequency during peak hours.
Route 181 will have improved weekday frequency and addition trips that run until midnight.
Route 182 will have earlier and later trips each day and will now be through-routed with Route 187.
Route 183 will add service on Sunday and run earlier and later on weekdays and Saturday.
Route 187 will be adjusted to run on 320th St and Hoyt Rd in both directions. The route will through-run with Route 182.

DART Route 902 is a new route that will replace DART Route 901. Route 902 has a DART service area in Mirror Lake. Every Route 902 trip will continue to/from a Route 903 trip. DART Route 903 offers a southern route via SW Campus Dr back to Federal Way Downtown station. Route 903 will have increased frequency with trips running every 30 minutes.

King County Metro is introducing two new Metro Flex pilot areas in Federal Way and Auburn. The Federal Way area is anchored at Federal Way Downtown station while the Auburn area is set near Auburn station and transit center.

Pierce Transit’s network is relatively stable for this restructure. Route 11 is getting a new northbound trip at 2pm on weekdays and several other trip times have been adjusted to accommodate the new trip. Route 212 will have a new southbound trip on Sundays at 7:08pm. Pierce Transit is also adding a new westbound trip to Route 214 on Sundays at 8:44am. The agency is also adjusting the schedules for an assortment of routes to improve reliability and reduce transfer times. Sound Transit is removing routes 580 and 586 in Pierce County.

South King and Pierce Counties have two big changes in overnight service. The A Line will now run every 30 minutes between midnight and 4am. Sound Transit is replacing Route 570 with Route 597. Route 597 will provide night-owl service every 30 minutes between Lakewood and Seattle, via Tacoma Dome and SeaTac.

paras: Once a quiet working-class Nordic-American neighborhood, Ballard is now a nightlife, shopping, and restaurant destination. Boutiques and cocktail bars line Ballard Avenue (home to one of Seattle’s few year-round farmers markets ), and townhomes and high-rises have taken the place of single-family homes. Some of the best restaurants and bars in the city can be found here, along with almost (almost!) too many breweries , which is why if you walk far enough inland you can literally smell the hops. Where else in Seattle can you find Detroit-style pizza, Sri Lankan cocktails, and a congee specialist?

articles.title: The Best Seafood Restaurants in Seattle
articles.author: <name>Mark DeJoy</name>
paras: Seattle is synonymous with seafood, and anyone who visits from out of town naturally wants to know where the city’s best seafood is. But that’s a tricky question. There are some self-described “seafood restaurants,” but fish and shellfish work their way into nearly every menu around Puget Sound. This includes oysters on the half shell at too many happy hours to count, crab and geoduck served as high-end delicacies, and sandwiches where freshly caught salmon or tuna is the star ingredient. A “best seafood in Seattle” map would pretty much just be a map of Seattle. So consider this a sampler platter of some of what the city has to offer across several different styles of cuisine and price point.

paras: Often thought of as Seattle’s southern little sister, Tacoma has surged in population in the last decade, and Washington State’s third-largest city can definitely hold its own against its siblings when it comes to its food scene. articles.title: An Eater’s Guide to Seattle
articles.author: <name>Sophie Grossman</name>
paras: Seattle is nestled in one of the most beautiful regions of North America. On clear days, you can look west over Puget Sound to see the Olympic Mountains and east across Lake Washington to the Cascades. The metro area is home to immigrant communities from all over Asia as well as Mexico, Central America, Ethiopia, and Somalia; there is also a substantial Indigenous population here. The cultural and ethnic diversity, combined with the wide range of local ingredients, makes the area a fertile ground for restaurants.

Owning a restaurant is a financially risky proposition in the best of times, and area owners are struggling with rising costs, especially now that the tipped minimum wage has expired in Seattle . But that hasn’t dampened the creativity of local chefs: 2025 saw a wave of exciting restaurant openings, and noteworthy new spots are always popping up . Here is a guide to the city’s ever-changing dining scene.

Washington is an agriculturally rich state, and Seattle restaurants benefit from an abundance of nearby farms, fruit orchards , fisheries, shellfish farms , ranches, and wineries . But the city is most famous for its seafood. Salmon is such a part of the area’s culinary identity that in the past, Sea-Tac Airport literally rolled out a red carpet for the first Copper River salmon of the season to arrive from Alaska. Shellfish is a Seattle staple, with many places serving oysters plucked out of its surrounding cold, nutrient-rich waterways. One local delicacy-bordering-on-novelty is the humble geoduck (pronounced “gooey duck”), an enormous clam that sometimes catches newcomers off guard because it looks like a penis.

Seattle features many great cuisines but is perhaps known best for its Asian restaurants. The city has an exceptional Japanese food scene and is home to world-class sushi masters — most notably Shiro Kashiba — and sustainable sushi pioneers like Taichi Kitamura. Pho is ubiquitous around town , and teriyaki — that sticky-sweet Japanese American dish — is a Seattle specialty, popularized by Toshihiro Kasahara at Toshi’s Teriyaki Restaurant in the 1970s (Kasahara still makes teriyaki at his latest restaurant, which is up north in Mill Creek). The Chinese restaurant scene is diversifying to include more regional cuisines, such as Sichuan . Bubble tea is also ubiquitous, and you can find some excellent options at old-school spot Seattle Best Tea or the University District location of Taiwanese chain Don’t Yell At Me . (The U District runneth over with bubble tea.)

But perhaps the hottest cuisine in Seattle is Filipino. Filipino immigrants have lived here since the 19th century, and Pike Place institution Oriental Mart is a testament to the longtime influence of Filipino cuisine. However, in the past half-decade, there’s been an explosion of innovative restaurants, like Melissa Miranda’s Musang and Aaron Verzosa and Amber Manuguid’s Archipelago (the latter of which was nominated for a 2025 James Beard Award ). There is also a bevy of buzzy but more casual Filipino-influenced spots, like the Chicken Supply , Moto Pizza , Hood Famous Bake Shop , and Ludi’s Restaurant .
Eater publishes plenty of maps detailing the top places and things to eat and drink in Seattle. Here are a few of our most popular guides to help you get started:

New Restaurants: This list changes every two months and includes restaurants that have opened or reopened in the last six months. Right now, notable new spots include the biang biang noodle champion Lily Wu’s waterfront seafood boil spot, Happy Crab ; Pioneer Square pastry shop and summer soft-serve stop the Pastry Project ; and new-wave Italian American restaurant Uncle Dom’s Italian Kitchen .

Essential Restaurants: If you need to narrow down the quarterly guide to Seattle’s 38 standout dining destinations even further, you might start at Off Alley , a 14-seat restaurant in a renovated brick alleyway in Columbia City, with its hyper-seasonal French-inflected small plates, excellent natural wines, and punk rock soundtrack. For something more casual, head to 40-year-old Beacon Hill standby Billiard Hoang for some of the city’s best pho and banh mi, plus a round of pool. Renee Erickson’s Sea Creatures restaurant group has come to define PNW cuisine in the past couple of decades, and her oyster bar, the Walrus and the Carpenter , is a must-visit. And you can’t forget about Communion , the soul food restaurant in the Central District from chef Kristi Brown.

Bakeries: One underrated aspect of Washington State’s agricultural prowess is the high-quality wheat that’s grown here. That local flour fuels an abundance of creative bakeries , some of which straddle the line between bakery, coffee shop, and restaurant, like Saint Bread in the University District, which was named a top bakery in the U.S. by the New York Times in 2024, and its sister cafe, the Wayland Mill . Some draw on Scandinavian baking traditions, like Queen Anne’s Byen Bakeri , while others are Asian-influenced, like the CID’s Fuji Bakery and Paper Cake Shop in Fremont, where you can get slab-style sheet-cake slices. Ben’s Bread in Phinney Ridge is a sourdough destination, and on Wednesday nights, it serves pizza that reliably and justifiably draws a massive line (you can only place an order in person).

Bars: Seattle’s bar scene is marked by countless dives , elegant cocktail lounges, and everything in between . Cocktail standouts include James Beard-semifinalist Rob Roy ; Canon , which features the nation’s largest spirits list; and Zig Zag Café , a Pike Place Market bar and restaurant where the Last Word, a famous cocktail, was reintroduced to the world by bartender Murray Stenson . And Pacific Inn , which is famous for its fish and chips , the Central District’s Twilight Exit , and Ballard institution Hattie’s Hat are some of the city’s most treasured dives. Seattle also boasts wine bars and bottle shops galore , like La Dive , a playful Capitol Hill hub for natural wine, and Le Caviste , which feels like a little slice of Paris bistro culture in Downtown Seattle.

Breweries: There’s been an exciting proliferation of breweries throughout Seattle in recent years, but Holy Mountain , with its constantly changing menu of offbeat, barrel-aged beers, is a must-visit. Cloudburst , just north of Pike Place Market, is a masterful maker of award-winning IPAs . Many breweries, too, have become hosts for Seattle’s many thriving food pop-ups , particularly Ballard’s Fair Isle Brewing . Relatively new entrant Project 9 Brewing has drawn acclaim for its wide array of beer styles, while Bizarre Brewing ’s complex, low-ABV brews have quickly become a mainstay among day-drinking beer dads.

Coffee: Seattle’s coffee shops run the gamut from lived-in hangouts that have been there for decades to trendy, new-wave espresso spots focused on lighter roasts and more diverse flavor profiles. Recently, a young generation of coffee lovers has brought renewed appreciation for Vietnamese-style phin-brewed coffee, which you can find at places like Hello Em and Phin in the International District, Coffeeholic House in Columbia City, and Fremont’s Aroom , which recently opened a second location on the city’s newly revitalized waterfront. Coffee originated in East Africa, and several spots around town are rooted in the deep-seated coffee traditions from that part of the world. You can experience an Ethiopian coffee ceremony at Lands of Origin in Pike Place Market, try specialty single-origin brews at Avole , or grab an excellent cup at one of Boon Boona ’s many locations around the city.

Views: You can’t help but notice the sparkling scenery in and around this fetching city, but some restaurants boast particularly stunning views . Ferry across Elliott Bay to dine on Hawaiian-Korean creations at Marination Ma Kai or nab an Adirondack chair on the north end of Lake Union for oysters and a skyline view at Westward .

Pike Place Market: If you’re visiting Downtown Seattle or taking a tour of the city with out-of-towners, chances are you’ll end up at Pike Place at some point . While Pike Place might have a touristy reputation, don’t let that deter you. It’s possible to take in the extravagant fish-tossing and partake in some of Seattle’s best food, whether that be the aforementioned lo-fi Filipino dining pioneer Oriental Mart or ultra-dramatic Italian American restaurant, the Pink Door , with its spinach lasagna and occasional trapeze artists.
These are the key areas of the city every self-proclaimed food lover has to survey — complete with what to eat and drink in each.

Capitol Hill is Seattle’s historically LGBTQ neighborhood and a nightlife hub. Though it’s contending with gentrification , it’s still home to many colorful queer businesses. It’s also one of Seattle’s best dining neighborhoods. See some of the finest options in our neighborhood guide . For Mexican, don’t miss Carmelo’s Tacos ; for Laotian, see Taurus Ox , which now has a burger-only spinoff restaurant, Ox Burger . A relative newcomer to the neighborhood, Ramie is making some of the most exciting and innovative moves in haute Vietnamese cuisine at the moment. If you are in the market for a high-end experience, Lark is a fine dining restaurant that is still doing it right, while LTD Edition Sushi is one of the city’s top omakase counters.

The Chinatown-International District (also known by shortened names like the CID, the International District, or the ID) is home to Chinatown, Japantown, Filipino Town, and Little Saigon, as well as too many incredible restaurants to name here. See our neighborhood dining guide for tons of options. For something more immersive, the Wing Luke Museum runs a food walking tour that is a great opportunity to learn about the rich history of the CID through the lens of its diverse cuisine. Gan Bei is a perfect late-night hangout for beer, Chinese fried chicken, and sausage clay pots, while Saigon Vietnam Deli is a great spot for a quick banh mi. The Thai restaurant E-Jae Pak Mor is famous for its dumplings with paper-thin skin . Don’t forget Tai Tung , Seattle’s oldest Chinese restaurant, founded in 1935. But for many locals, the top reason to go to the CID is the massive Asian supermarket Uwajimaya , which sells an array of products and also has plenty of hot food counters and a food court.

Once a rough-and-tumble Scandinavian fishing village, 21st-century Ballard is now startlingly hip. The neighborhood — mapped out for your dining convenience — straddles the line between modern development and the preservation of its early history. There’s plenty worth eating here, including wood-fired pizza perfectionist Delancey and Lebanese restaurant Cafe Munir . Little Beast , Eater Seattle’s 2025 restaurant of the year , takes English pub food to new heights with its meticulously sourced and prepared meats. The neighborhood also has its own brewery district with more than a dozen brewers within walking distance, including Reuben’s , Stoup , and Urban Family .

Georgetown has a history of grit and brick, but has also become a thriving culinary and cultural destination, fostering a local character that draws in visitors from all over town. You can find decadent slices of cakes at Deep Sea Sugar and Salt , wonderful vegan sandwiches at the divey Georgetown Liquor Company , top-notch handmade pasta in a romantic setting at Mezzanotte , and intricate six-course prix fixe meals at the Corson Building .

This eclectic neighborhood (see: massive troll under a bridge ), just north of Lake Union, and to the east of Ballard, harbors a fair share of standout restaurants: Chef Mutsuko Soma’s soba destination Kamonegi , the French-ish Le Coin , and Local Tide , where people line up for the succulent crab rolls, in particular. James Beard Award-winning chefs Rachel Yang and Seif Chirchi run the kitchen at Joule , known for its kalbi short ribs, local pickled vegetables, and a fresh take on Korean cuisine. If you want something sweet, check out Doce , which serves massive brioche-style doughnuts and has quickly expanded to three locations since opening in 2023 .

West Seattle’s dining scene and the picturesque Alki Beach are equally impressive. You’ll find inventive dinners using hyper-local ingredients at Driftwood , fantastic pasta in a century-old log house at Il Nido , and top-notch smoked meats at Lady Jaye , which also boasts a terrific backyard patio. Seafood fans should check out Mashiko for sushi that emphasizes sustainability; those recovering from a long night can eat breakfast (or get some hair of the dog) with a side of killer soundtrack at Easy Street Records & Cafe .
Central District , U District , Tacoma , and Seattle-Tacoma International Airport .

It’s a hot dog or sausage slathered in — wait for it — cream cheese and grilled onions. The murky origin story goes back to the late 1990s, when a bagel cart in Pioneer Square went a little rogue . Though it sounds strange, the sweet and meaty flavor combination is surprisingly satisfying (try some hot sauce on it), and even high-end restaurants will sometimes riff on the concoction for specials. You can generally find a Seattle dog at Capitol Hill stands bumping Latin dance music and selling the franks late into the night along with elotes, and at other hot dog-focused places around town .

This sticky-sweet Japanese-American dish is a Seattle specialty, popularized by Toshihiro Kasahara at Toshi’s Teriyaki Restaurant in the 1970s. You can still find Kasahara north of the city at Toshi’s Teriyaki Grill in Mill Creek; within Seattle city limits, try gluten-free options at West Seattle’s Grillbird Teriyaki .

Old-school yet relevant, Canlis is Seattle’s archetypal fine dining restaurant, which has shown a great deal of versatility over the years. In 2025, the restaurant shook up its ownership structure (now the sole owner is Mark Canlis) and suffered a much-talked-about negative review in The Seattle Times . But whoever is at the helm, Canlis remains one of the city’s most important restaurants.

This James Beard Award-winning chef channels rustic European country cooking by way of seasonal Pacific Northwest ingredients in her bright, airy, elegant spaces. She runs some of the city’s most adored spots through her Sea Creatures restaurant group, including oyster bar, the Walrus and the Carpenter, and Westward . Despite controversy over staff unionization efforts , which coincided with the closure of several restaurants in 2025, her empire continues to grow: She recently opened three new restaurants in Pioneer Square, Lowlander Brewing , Un Po Tipsy , and Mio Oh Mio . Meanwhile, her innovative Capitol Hill steakhouse Bateau, which has been closed since summer 2025, has rebranded as Jeffry’s and recently reopened with a similar menu.

A legend in his own right, this beloved chef trained with Jiro Ono (of Jiro Dreams of Sushi ) before bringing Edomae-style sushi to Seattle and defining the scene here over the past 50 years. He spent early days at Maneki and other spots around town, pioneering the use of local seafood, then two decades at namesake Shiro’s . Finally, after the world’s shortest retirement, Kashiba returned to the counter in late 2015 at Pike Place Market’s Sushi Kashiba , where you can still find him on Wednesdays and Saturdays. He’s now focused on helping the next generation of Seattle sushi chefs open their own restaurants.
